clue.text: Text-moving facility can put dates differently

indicators.note: doing something differently means arranging it another way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A word-processing feature could rearrange calendar dates.
explanation.definitionFit: Cut and paste is the editing function that lifts a block of text from one place and drops it in another.

clue.text: Separate sculpture at college

parts.note: to sculpture something is to carve it
a student at university is said to be up

explanation.surface: A piece of sculpture stands apart in a college quad.
explanation.walkthrough: Being UP means being in residence at a university, especially Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: To carve up is to divide something into portions, splitting it apart among several parties.

clue.text: In Yorkshire reportedly, the pointer that's used for forecasting?

definitions.note: read as 'that which is used for forecasting', a noun phrase

indicators.note: the words are to be heard as a Yorkshire speaker says them, clipping 'the' to a t' sound

parts.note: Yorkshire dialect shortens 'the' to t', and an arrow is a pointer

explanation.surface: A wry question about a Yorkshire weather vane's arrow.
explanation.walkthrough: In Yorkshire speech 'the arrow' comes out as 't'arrow', which sounds like the card name.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarot cards are dealt by fortune-tellers to predict what lies ahead.

clue.text: Name names unexpectedly, drinking with journalist

indicators.note: a drinker takes something inside, so the rearranged letters swallow another piece
something that turns out unexpectedly is not in its predicted order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for name
taken as written
W is short for with

explanation.surface: Someone unexpectedly names names while out drinking with a reporter.
explanation.definitionFit: A newsman is a reporter or correspondent working for a newspaper or broadcaster.

clue.text: Alarm bleeper turboprop carries

indicators.note: the phrase carries the answer within it, spanning the join between two words

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: An aircraft's warning buzzer goes off on a propeller plane.
explanation.definitionFit: To alarm someone is to disturb or unsettle them, the same sense as perturb.

clue.text: I'll pay for letting reserve catch up with soldier, perhaps

parts.note: a sub is a substitute or reserve player

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to net is to catch
a soldier is one kind of ant

explanation.surface: A sports reserve comes off the bench to catch up with a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letting' here is renting out property, not permitting; the speaker is someone renting from a tenant.
explanation.definitionFit: A subtenant pays rent to the main tenant for a property sublet to them.

clue.text: Raised a Republican flag crossing East African state

indicators.note: crossing means the following words straddle the next piece, holding it between them
in a down clue, raised means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for East
R stands for Republican
to flag is to tire

explanation.surface: A Republican banner is hoisted on the way across eastern Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Eritrea is a country on the Red Sea coast in the Horn of Africa.

clue.text: Pilots and cabin staff boasted behind first-class customer's back

indicators.note: one piece comes behind, after, the others in the answer

parts.note: A1 is first-class, written AI in letters

indicators.note: the back of a word is its tail end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of customer
crew is a British past tense of crow, to boast

explanation.surface: Someone bragged behind the back of a premium passenger.
explanation.walkthrough: CREW as the past of crow is an older British form, used for a cock crowing and for boasting.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircrew is the whole team working on board a plane, both flight deck and cabin.

clue.text: Sweet manufactured as an edible line

indicators.note: something manufactured is made up from raw materials, so the letters are assembled into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A confectioner's product made as something you can eat.
explanation.walkthrough: An aniseed ball is a small, hard, aniseed-flavoured British sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet in British English is a piece of confectionery, what Americans call candy.

clue.text: Criticise waste

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to dismiss something as worthless, a verb
second meaning: refuse or trash, a noun

explanation.surface: An order to condemn the squandering of resources.
explanation.definitionFit: To rubbish an idea is to disparage it, and rubbish is also household refuse or garbage.

clue.text: Greek philosopher in Post Office with boxes

parts.note: in and hip both mean fashionable
the usual abbreviation
crates are wooden boxes

explanation.surface: An ancient thinker stands in a post office holding parcels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a placing word but supplies a synonym for trendy.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippocrates was the ancient Greek physician, and the clue loosely counts him among the philosophers of his era.

clue.text: Clumsy writer returns, inspired by Stephen King novel

indicators.note: breathed into, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: It is a 1986 horror novel by Stephen King

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word runs right to left

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: An awkward author returns to the page, influenced by a Stephen King book.
explanation.definitionFit: Inept describes someone lacking skill or competence, awkward in what they do.

clue.text: Mediocre cheese and game

definitions.meaning: first meaning: slang for bland, cheap cheese, good enough only to bait a trap
second meaning: a children's board game with a contraption that catches plastic mice

explanation.surface: A poor cheeseboard paired with a game, a dull evening in.
explanation.definitionFit: Mousetrap is jocular slang for low-grade cheddar, and also the name of a long-running board game.

clue.text: Describe former boyfriend Frank?

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
frank and plain both mean straightforward or candid

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to describe an ex-boyfriend named Frank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' with its capital looks like a man's name, but it is the adjective meaning candid.
explanation.definitionFit: To explain something is to set it out clearly, giving an account of it.

clue.text: Meat on tie awkward previously

indicators.note: something awkward is ungainly and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A food stain on a necktie used to be embarrassing.
explanation.definitionFit: At one time means formerly, in the past, the sense of previously.

clue.text: Take a bow, madam, and perform show

parts.note: brava is the cheer for a female performer
to do is to perform

explanation.surface: An actress is invited to bow and put on a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italian cheer has a masculine form BRAVO and a feminine form BRAVA; 'madam' asks for the feminine.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravado is a display of boldness, a show of courage meant to impress.

clue.text: Tried to upset City

indicators.note: upsetting something knocks it over and out of order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone attempted to unsettle a football club called City.
explanation.walkthrough: City looks like a team name, as in Manchester City, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Detroit is the largest city in Michigan, the home of the US car industry.

clue.text: Exceed speed at sea in hair-raising style

parts.note: to top is to surpass
a knot is a unit of speed used for ships

explanation.surface: Breaking a speed record at sea would be a terrifying ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hair-raising' usually means frightening, but here it is literal: a style that piles the hair up.
explanation.definitionFit: A topknot is a hairstyle with the hair gathered into a bun or tuft on top of the head.

clue.text: Instructs every one to enter brief trial

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word loses its last letter
entering means going inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a test is a trial, with its final letter dropped
each means every one

explanation.surface: A judge instructs all parties to attend a short hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Teaches and instructs both mean imparts knowledge or skill to someone.

clue.text: Exit, presumably, not under cover

definitions.meaning: first meaning, playful: a door leading out
second meaning: in the open air

explanation.surface: A sign by a door marks the way out to the open air.
explanation.definitionFit: Outdoor describes activities done in the open air, without a roof overhead.

clue.text: Month desperate reboot saves Mac at last

indicators.note: to save something is to keep it safe inside, so one piece is held within the other
a desperate state is a wild one, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter of Mac

explanation.surface: A frantic restart finally rescues an Apple computer.
explanation.definitionFit: October is the tenth month of the year.

clue.text: A few hours for public school runs?

definitions.text: A few hours for public school runs?

parts.words: A few hours for public school runs?
parts.note: surface reading: a short stint of cricket or running at a fee-paying British school

parts.words: A few hours for public school runs?
parts.note: setter's reading: a spell during which a school is run for members of the public to look around

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a public school is an elite private school, so 'public school' looks like one unit; split it, and the public come in while the school carries on.
explanation.definitionFit: An event day when an institution invites visitors in to see how it works is called this.

clue.text: Tech company getting hump? Better not upset it!

parts.note: Apple is the computer and phone maker
to hump and to cart both mean to lug something heavy

explanation.surface: A tech giant is having a sulk, so tread carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting the hump' is British for becoming sulky, but here hump is a verb meaning carry. The definition alludes to the idiom 'upset the applecart'.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset the applecart is to spoil a plan or arrangement, so this is the thing one should avoid overturning.

clue.text: Jazz trumpeter Baker accepts introduction to Acker Bilk

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so one piece goes inside the name

parts.note: Chet Baker was an American jazz trumpeter

indicators.note: an introduction is the opening, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of Acker

explanation.surface: One jazz musician welcomes another, clarinettist Acker Bilk.
explanation.walkthrough: Acker Bilk was a British jazz clarinettist, so 'Acker Bilk' reads as one name; the surname is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To bilk someone is to swindle or defraud them, which is to cheat.

clue.text: Coarse teen regularly missing class

indicators.note: missing at regular intervals means every other letter is dropped

parts.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: A rude teenager keeps skipping lessons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'class' looks like a school lesson but means a social rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A caste is a hereditary social class, especially in the Hindu system.

clue.text: Half of UK capital is in good hands initially, and fairly spread out

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the pair of initials
half of a word means keeping only one half and losing the rest

parts.note: the first half of London

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letters of the words before it

parts.note: the first letter of good
taken as written
the first letter of hands

explanation.surface: Half of London is in safe hands, and the city sprawls.
explanation.definitionFit: Longish means rather long, somewhat extended in length.

clue.text: Live Fringe show's opening as well

parts.note: to be is to live or exist
a fringe is an edge or side

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, which alone is kept

parts.note: the first letter of show

explanation.surface: Opening night of a live show at the Edinburgh Fringe festival.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fringe is the Edinburgh arts festival, but here it is just an edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Besides means in addition, also, the same as as well.

clue.text: Treatment of limbs by specialist suspended?

definitions.text: Treatment of limbs by specialist suspended?

parts.words: Treatment of limbs by specialist suspended?
parts.note: surface reading: an orthopaedic surgeon struck off from treating arms and legs

parts.words: Treatment of limbs by specialist suspended?
parts.note: setter's reading: a specialist hanging in a harness while cutting branches

explanation.walkthrough: 'Limbs' are branches, not arms and legs, and 'suspended' means hanging from ropes, not barred from work.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the trade of pruning, felling and caring for trees, done by an arborist who often climbs on ropes.
